[b]The Office of the President:  March 6th, 2025[/b]

The morning light poured the large windows of the presidential office, casting a joyful light around the grand office. A low fire burned in a decorated fireplace that sat against the far wall of the office opposite and to the right of the grand double doors which were flanked by two marble pillars. 

Consantin VI had spent the night with his family and allies celebrating the victory in the Chamber of the Peoples, a small affair compared to other parties, however, the affair had failed to ease his worries. There was no doubt that the people would react with outrage at their will being thwarted by pro-presidential politicians, and violence was without a doubt a possibility.

As a result of this he had called a meeting that morning with his top advisor and an old friend from the army, Janus Elbringer, a shrewd individual with a tactical mind that made him a dangerous asset and ally for Consantin. 

A small silver clock ticked away on Consantins desk, it had been a gift from his wife and son after the electoral victory he had secured six months prior in 2024. Janus was late.

After five minutes the right side door of the office finally opened and Janus stepped in. Janus did not look like your stereotypical schemer, he was an older gentleman with a kindly and warm face, although a nasty scar on the ear hinted at a rougher past.

You are late, stated Consantin bluntly.

Traffic mlord, replied Janus, bowing slightly.

Then travel by foot, replied Consantin, frowning slightly.

If only my friend, but my ailment prevents me, replied Janus referencing a nasty injury he had gotten on his leg during a protest that had left him slightly crippled.

Very well, have a seat, replied Consantin as Janus sat himself before the desk.

Your son pulled off a wonderful victory yesterday, wrangling that coalition so quickly, began Janus.

That he did, but I worry it wont last, replied Consantin, With the recent results, you and I both know that the opposition will try to stir the waters among the people, he continued.

Yes of course, seeing as they have failed to stir the waters in the Senate and Chamber of the Peoples, replied Janus.

In fact the intellect with which I have been given has shown me that they already are doing so, even before the vote yesterday, radicals in the mountains, plotting and scheming, stated Consantin.

There was a brief pause as Janus thought for a moment before replying, Could we get rid of these radicals? 

And what? Cause more to rise up, more copycats? Enquired Consantin, incredulous.

You make a fair point, replied Janus, leaning forward, his mind deep in thought.

Consantin rose from his desk, a hand placed on his brow as he sighed, turning to face the window, which led out to the balcony that faced the square before the palace he hung his head, I love our democracy, I love our republic, what must I do to keep it? he stated aloud.

Youre being fatalistic, replied Janus bluntly, Fatalism will not help you gain anything, he continued, rising from his seat to stand beside Consantin.

Now, with the cards back in our hands for now, we must move swiftly, he stated as the two men moved to sit down again. 

Yes of course, where can we move first? replied Consantin seemingly more alert. 

I would say that we move to keep our control in the Chamber of the Peoples, perhaps find a way to keep the coalition between the Presidential Party and the PoJ together, began Janus, pulling out a pen and notepad from his back pocket.

And the Senate? enquired Consantin, nodding along.

The Senate is split evenly, though we have the luck of Tito being Speaker, for now, however he is a bit weak for our purposes, replied Janus.

So we remove Tito, and replace him with another then, stated Consantin.

Yesmaybe, replied Janus tapping his pen upon the notepad.

Maybe? enquired Consantin raising an eyebrow.

I am just worried that removing him so soon before the assembling of the Chamber of Unity in two months would cause an uproar in the Senate and weaken our position there, replied Janus.

So we wait then, and at the Chamber of Unity, we remove him, formally, ceremonially, nodded Consantin in agreement.

Yes, that might be our best bet, he is already unpopular with three members of the Senate due to his tie breaking vote, perhaps we could exploit that over the next two months, put some pressure on him, replied Janus.

Alright, I like where this is going, replied Consantin, Practical, and low risk, he stated.

Another note, began Janus, causing Consantin to raise his eyebrow once more, What is your plan for security at the speech next week? Janus enquired.

Well given the potential presence of protestors, and even radicals, Id say high security, replied Consantin.

Janus frowned at this and wrote some notes in his notepad, To be frank, I do not like this, I do not believe having a public speech so soon and close to such a divisive vote as yesterdays would be beneficial to you or to order, he stated, Is there anyway we can move this to be a televised address? he enquired.

Televised? stated Consantin in slight shock, My dear friend, the speech is meant to bring the chambers into unity, and show a united front and government, he replied, surprised at the suggestion.

Yes, however, I fear, began Janus before being cut off by Consantin.
Bah! Alright, Ill consider moving it to a televised speech, he replied waving his hand dismissively, Its not like Id have a choice, he stated gruffly.

Very good, when can I expect your formal decision sir? enquired Janus.

Give me a day, you should have it, replied Consantin, Anything else? he asked.

No sir, I think that is all for now, I will contact you if anything comes up, replied Janus, rising from the chair to shake Consantins hand.

Very good, very good, replied Consantin returning the handshake before moving to let Janus out of the office. 

Once Janus had gone Consantin moved back to his desk and sat down once more, quietly he phoned his son Mikael to secure some details for the speech, he wasnt about to be threatened by a bunch of small minded protestors.

[b]2025: A day in Etherniasti[/b]

Minister Olym Vass stepped out of his apartment, his uniform neatly pressed, and took a deep breath of the crisp morning air. Etherniasti was thriving, its economy humming like a well-oiled machine. The uranium mines operated at peak efficiency, soda sales were at an all-time high, and the beef-based agricultural sector had just announced a new line of protein-packed government-issued steaks.

The nation prided itself on social equality, and nowhere was this more evident than in its strict economic policies. Private enterprise was outlawed, ensuring that no citizen could amass great wealth while another suffered. Everyone had enough, and no one had too much. It was a philosophy that had made Etherniasti the envy of socialist economists and the bane of capitalist critics, who decried its lack of entrepreneurial spirit.

Olym made his way to the Ministry of Law & Order, nodding at the officers patrolling the streets. Crime was virtually unknown in Etherniasti, a testament to the nations well-funded police force and its progressive welfare policies. Every citizen had access to free education, healthcare, and housing, ensuring that desperation never took root. The only arrests made in the last year were for minor infractionsone man had attempted to sell homemade furniture, a clear violation of the state industry laws. He was now gainfully employed at the National Chair Restoration Facility, his skills put to proper use.

As Olym entered the ministry, his assistant handed him the morning reports. Public intoxication had reached record lows since the banning of fraternities, and the government's talent screening for Etherniastis Got Talent had ensured that the show was now watchable. The only ongoing concern was the national animalthe dodowhose numbers had dwindled precariously due to deforestation caused by expanding uranium mines. Efforts to establish a Dodo Preservation Program had stalled, as no one could agree on whether the birds were worth saving if they refused to adapt to modern industry.

The daily referendum results came in at noon. The citizens had spoken: the national anthem would not be extended. Olym sighedhe had rather liked the idea of a verse about agriculture. But that was democracy in Etherniasti. Every voice mattered, every decision was made by the people, and every soda sold was state-approved. Life was orderly, predictable, and unquestionably patriotic.
